pieces.name: Service retirees: 11,271 retired officers

source.doc: PABF Actuarial Valuation as of 12/31/2025 (Lewis & Ellis), Exhibits B, D, E, F, G; PABF Financial Statements 2025 p.17
source.note: Annual benefits by group: Exhibit E service retirees $914,683,048 (p.50), Exhibit F widows $94,059,866 (p.51), Exhibit G miscellaneous annuities (p.52); these add to $1,032,071,723 in Exhibit B (p.44). Death benefits $1,991,600 and refunds $11,718,221 are 2025 payments from the financial statements p.17. 110 refund payments in Exhibit D (pp.48-49).

pieces.unit_label: retired officers (share of the City's payment each)
pieces.note: Proxy: this group draws $914,683,048 a year in benefits, 87.46% of the $1,045,781,544 of benefit dollars (annual annuities in force at 12/31/2025 plus 2025 death benefits and refunds). Average benefit $81,154 a year per person. Exhibit E (p.50). The City's payment is not the same as the benefits paid. The City sends one payment set by law to the fund, and the fund pays its retirees from that money plus member contributions and investment earnings. This split shares the payment out by each group's share of yearly benefit dollars, so it is our estimate, not a City figure.
pieces.why: The City's payment goes to the fund as one lump sum, and thousands of retirees in this group share it, so each person's share is far under $1M and no single person's benefit is bought by one payment.

pieces.name: Advance payment: City pays more than State law requires

source.doc: PABF Actuarial Valuation as of 12/31/2025 (Lewis & Ellis) p.10

pieces.why: This is money the City chooses to pay on top of what the law requires, so the fund has more savings and the shortfall grows more slowly, and it goes into the fund as one payment.
pieces.note: Under the City's Pension Management Policy (2022) the City budgets extra payments on top of the State-law minimum so the shortfall does not grow. The valuation lists the extras actually paid and assumes no more in its projections.
